title: CLR/132/2017 of Smt Sushil Kaur Harbans Singh Chug Vs Waqf No 12-a AND OTHERS

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND
AT NAINITAL
CIVIL REVISION No. 132 of 2017
Smt. Sushil Kaur Harbans Singh Chug ... Defendant/Revisionist

Versus
WAQF No. 12-A & Others ......Plaintiff/Respondents
Present: Mr. Neeraj Garg, Advocate for the revisionist
Mr. Siddhartha Singh, Advocate for the respondent No. 2.
Mr. Ahrar Baig, Advocate holding brief of Ms. Nishat
Intezar, Advocate for respondent No. 3
Hon'ble Sharad Kumar Sharma, J. (Oral)
 This is a revision under Section 25 of the
Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, 1887 (hereinafter to be
called as an Act) wherein, in a SCC Suit No. 32 of 2009 -
Waqf No. 12-A and another Versus Smt. Sushil Kaur &
another. The suit of the plaintiff has been decreed by the
impugned judgment dated 18.09.2017 and consequent
thereto the present revisionist has been directed to vacate
the premises and to pay the arrears of rent and damages
as determined by the said Court. Challenging the said
judgment dated 18.09.2017, the instant revision has been
preferred by the revisionist-tenant before this Court.
2. This revision was directed to be heard on the
admission, before being admitted, this Court issued
notices and summoned the Lower Court Records. Both the
parties agree that let the revision itself be decided on
merits. Accordingly, the revision is admitted and
simultaneously it was taken up yesterday for final hearing

2
and after hearing both the counsel at length, the matter
has been placed today for dictation of judgment.
3. Learned counsel for the revisionist has made an
attempt by placing vexed question of law, though it may
not be emanating in accordance with the circumstances of
the case. What has been tried to be argued by the learned
counsel for the revisionist may be summed up on three
vital issues:-
(i) He submits that since the property is a Waqf property,
in that view of the matter, the proceedings ought to
have been taken before the Tribunal in view of the
provisions contained under Section 83 read with
Section 85 of the Waqf Act.
(ii) He further submits that on account of the fact that the
recipient of the rent was plaintiff/respondent No. 2,
hence the relationship of landlord and tenant, if any, it
existed between the plaintiff/respondent No. 2 and
not with the plaintiff/respondent No. 1.
(iii) He submits that a deliberate effort has been made by
impleading plaintiff/respondent No. 1 so as to oust the
jurisdiction of Act No. 13 of 1972.
4. This Court feels that all these three issues are to
be dealt independently. Accordingly, the first issue
pertaining to the impact of plaintiff/respondent No. 1 being
Waqf is being determined at this stage.
5. Before addressing on merits, what is remarkably
to be seen in the pleadings of tenant is that the status of
the plaintiffs and their status as a landlord have not been
controverted by the tenant in his written statement at the

3
first instance when tenant had the opportunity in any
specific terms. His contention is to the effect that the
proceedings ought to have been initiated by the plaintiffs
under Section 83 read with Section 85 under the Waqf Act
and as such the proceedings before the SCC Court was
not maintainable. This argument as extended by Mr.
Neeraj Garg, learned counsel for the revisionist cannot be
accepted. There are few justified reasons for the same:-
(i) For the purposes of invocation of Section 83 of the
Waqf Act, it provides to deal with the disputes or
question or matters relating to the Waqf or Waqf
property under this Act.
(ii) The arguments about the maintainability of the
proceedings on the ground that it should have been
initiated before the Tribunal under Section 83 read
with Section 85 of the Waqf Act cannot be accepted,
the reason being under Section 83 deals with
disputes of Waqf or Waqf property. Here in the
present case, there is no dispute about the status of
property being waqf property. Rather the pleading of
revisnist that proceedings ought to be drawn before
Tribunal, created under Waqf Act, itself in an
admission it is a waqf property, but there is no dispute
of property. Proceedings for eviction of tenant from
the waqf property by invoking under Section 15 of the
Act, itself cannot be termed as to be disputed related
to waqf property, as it would be dispute of tenant and
landlord and not regards to title of property.
(ii) It also relates to the settlement of a dispute pertaining
to the Mutwalli and other disputes as contemplated
therein.
(iii) Under Section 83(2) in regard to the dispute as to
who would be entitled to function as mutwalli. Thus
the prerogative of proceedings under Section 83(2) is
with the person who claims to be mutwally is

4
aggrieved by an order having a bearing on the file of
the mutwalli, this is not the issue involved in the
present case.
 Nature of dispute under Section 83, is covered by sub
Section (1) and (2) of Section 83, which could be
adjudicated by Tribunal created under Section
83(3)(4).
Section 83 of the Waqf Act, 1995 is quoted herein
below :
83. Constitution of Tribunals, etc.-
2[(1) The State Government shall, by notification in the
Official Gazette, constitute as many Tribunals as it may think
fit, for the determination of any dispute, question or other
matter relating to a waqf or waqf property, eviction of a tenant
or determination of rights and obligations of the less or and
the lessee of such property, under this Act and define the local
limits and jurisdiction of such Tribunals;]
(2) Any mutawalli person interested in a 1[waqf] or any other
person aggrieved by an order made under this Act, or rules
made thereunder, may make an application within the time
specified in this Act or where no such time has been specified,
within such time as may be prescribed, to the Tribunal for the
determination of any dispute, question or other matter
relating to the 1[waqf]
(3) Where any application made under sub-section (1) relates
to any 1[waqf] property which falls within the territorial limits
of the jurisdiction of two or more Tribunals, such application
may be made to the Tribunal within the local limits of whose
jurisdiction the mutawalli or any one of the mutawallis of the
1[waqf] actually and voluntarily resides, carries on business or
personally works for gain, and, where any such application is
made to the Tribunal aforesaid, the other Tribunal or
Tribunals having jurisdiction shall not entertain any
application for the determination of such dispute, question or
other matter:
Provided that the State Government may, if it is of opinion
that it is expedient in the interest of the 1[waqf] or any other
person interested in the 1[waqf] or the 1[waqf] property to
transfer such application to any other Tribunal having
jurisdiction for the determination of the dispute, question or
other matter relating to such 1[waqf] or 1[waqf] property,
transfer such application to any other Tribunal having
jurisdiction, and, on such transfer, the Tribunal to which the

5
application is so transferred shall deal with the application
from the stage which was reached before the Tribunal from
which the application has been so transferred, except where
the Tribunal is of opinion that it is necessary in the interests of
justice to deal with the application afresh.
3[(4) Every Tribunal shall consist of--
(a) one person, who shall be a member of the State Judicial
Service holding a rank, not below that of a District, Sessions or
Civil Judge, Class I, who shall be the Chairman;
(b) one person, who shall be an officer from the State Civil
Services equivalent in rank to that of the Additional District
Magistrate, Member;
(c) one person having knowledge of Muslim law and
jurisprudence, Member,
and the appointment of every such person shall be made
either by name or by designation.
(4A) The terms and conditions of appointment including the
salaries and allowances payable to the Chairman and other
members other than persons appointed as ex officio members
shall be such as may be prescribed.]
(5) The Tribunal shall be deemed to be a civil court and shall
have the same powers as may be exercised by a civil court
under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908), while
trying a suit, or executing a decree or order.
(6) Notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Civil
Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908), the Tribunal shall follow such
procedure as may be prescribed.
(7) The decision of the Tribunal shall be final and binding
upon the parties to the application and it shall have the force
of a decree made by a civil court.
(8) The Execution of any decision of the Tribunal shall be
made by the civil court to which such decision is sent for
execution in accordance with the provisions of the Code of
Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908).
(9) No appeal shall lie against any decision or order whether
interim or otherwise, given or made by the Tribunal:
Provided that a High Court may, on its own motion or on the
application of the Board or any person aggrieved, call for and
examine the records relating to any dispute, question or other
matter which has been determined by the Tribunal for the
purpose of satisfying itself as to the correctness, legality or
propriety of such determination and may conform, reviews or

6
modify such determination or pass such other orders as it may
think fit.
6. If we scrutinize the provisions of Section 83 and
read the same in consonance to the provisions contained
under Section 7 of the Waqf Act, 1995 which deals with
the power of the Tribunal to determine a dispute relates to
the inter se dispute as narrated in the said provision.
Section 7 of the Waqf Act, 1995 is quoted herein below:
Section 7 - Power of Tribunal to determine disputes
regarding waqf

(1) If, after the commencement of this Act, 1[any question or
dispute] arises, whether a particular property specified as
5[waqf] property in a list of 4[auqaf] is 5[waqf] property or
not, or whether a 5[waqf] specified in such list is a Shia
5[waqf] or a Sunni 5[waqf], the Board or the mutawalli of the
5[waqf], 2[or any person aggrieved by the publication of the
list of auqaf under section 5] therein, may apply to the
Tribunal having jurisdiction in relation to such property, for
the decision of the question and the decision of the Tribunal
thereon shall be final:
Provided that-
(a) in the case of the list of 4[auqaf] relating to any part
of the State and published after the commencement of
this Act no such application shall be entertained after
the expiry of one year from the date of publication of
the list of 4[auqaf]; and
(b) in the case of the list of 4[auqaf] relating to any part
of the State and published at any time within a period of
one year immediately preceding the commencement of
this Act, such an application may be entertained by
Tribunal within the period of one year from such
commencement:
Provided further that where any such question has been heard
and finally decided by civil court in a suit instituted before
such commencement, the Tribunal shall not re-open such
question.
(2) Except where the Tribunal has no jurisdiction by reason of
the provisions of sub-section (5), no proceeding under this
section in respect of any 5[waqf] shall be stayed by any court,
tribunal or other authority by reason only of the pendency of

7
any suit, application or appeal or other proceeding arising out
of any such suit, application, appeal or other proceeding.
(3) The Chief Executive Officer shall not be made a party to
any application under subsection (1).
(4) The list of 4[auqaf] and where any such list is modified in
pursuance of a decision of the Tribunal under sub-section (1),
the list as so modified, shall be final.
(5) The Tribunal shall not have jurisdiction to determine any
matter which is the subject-matter of any suit or proceeding
instituted or commenced in a civil court under sub-section (1)
of section 6, before the commencement of this Act or which is
the subject-matter of any appeal from the decree passed
before such commencement in any such suit or proceeding or
of any application for revision or review arising out of such
suit, proceeding or appeal, as the case may be.
3[(6) The Tribunal shall have the powers of assessment of
damages by unauthorised occupation of waqf property and to
penalise such unauthorised occupants for their illegal
occupation of the waqf property and to recover the damages as
arrears of land revenue through the Collector:
Provided that whosoever, being a public servant, fails in his
lawful duty to prevent or remove an encroachment, shall on
conviction be punishable with fine which may extend to fifteen
thousand rupees for each such offence.]
7. If we read Section 83 and 7 together, it does not
encompass within itself a settlement of any dispute by
virtue of which an eviction of a tenant is sought from an
accommodation belonging to waqf which has been leased
out to him in the capacity of the tenant, is not the case of
revisionist that he is not tenant over waqf property, he
disputes forum of proceedings and thus the argument
which has been extended by the learned counsel for the
revisionist that the eviction proceedings ought to have
been taken under Section 83 before the Tribunal created
under the Waqf Act is not acceptable to this Court.

8
8. To refute the arguments as extended by the
learned counsel for the revisionist, the learned counsel for
the plaintiffs-respondents has placed reliance on a
judgment rendered as by the Hon'ble Apex Court as
reported in 2010 (3) SCC (Civil) 553 in Ramesh
Gobindram (Dead) through LRS. Vs. Sugra Humayun
Mirza Wakf. The Hon'bel Apex Court has laid down that
since under the Waqf Act, there is no provision for eviction
of a tenant from a premises which has been leased out to
the tenant over a property which belongs to the Waqf
eviction suit against such tenant is held only to be
maintainable before the Civil Court and not before the
Tribunal, created under the Waqf Act. Hon'ble Apex Court
in its para Nos. 2, 4, 11, 25, 33 and 35 held as under:
"2. The question is whether the Wakf Tribunal constituted under
Section 83 of the Wakf Act, 1995 was competent to entertain and
adjudicate upon disputes regarding eviction of the appellants who are
occupying different items of what are admittedly Wakf properties. The
Wakf Tribunal before whom the suits for eviction of the tenants were
filed answered the question regarding its jurisdiction in the affirmative
and decreed the suit filed against the appellant.
4. Whether or not the Wakf Tribunal can entertain and adjudicate
upon a dispute regarding eviction of a tenant holding wakf property
under the Wakf Board, would depend upon the scheme of the Wakf
Act, 1995 and express or implied exclusion of the jurisdiction of the
Civil Courts to entertain any such dispute. If the Act excludes the
jurisdiction of the Civil Courts whether such exclusion is absolute and
all pervasive or limited only to a particular class of disputes is also an
incidental question that may have to be addressed. There is a cleavage
in the judicial opinion expressed on these questions by different High
Courts in the country.
11. Before we take up the core issue whether the jurisdiction of Civil
Court to entertain and adjudicate upon disputes regarding eviction of
wakf property stands excluded under the Wakf Act we may briefly
outline the approach that the Courts have to adopt while dealing with
such questions.
25. Whenever a question arises whether "any dispute, question or other
matter" relating to "any wakf or wakf property or other matter" falls

9
within the jurisdiction of a Civil Court the answer would depend upon
whether any such dispute, question or other matter is required under the
Act to be determined by the Tribunal constituted under the Act. If the
answer be in the affirmative, the jurisdiction of Civil Court would be
excluded qua such a question, for in that case the Tribunal alone can
entertain and determine any such question. The bar of jurisdiction
contained in Section 85 is in that sense much wider than that contained
in Section 6(5) read with Section 7 of the Wakf Act. While the latter
bars the jurisdiction of the Civil Court only in relation of questions
specified in Sections 6(1) and 7(1), the bar of jurisdiction contained in
Section 85 would exclude the jurisdiction of the Civil Courts not only
in relation to matters that specifically fall in Sections 6 and 7 but also
other matters required to be determined by a Tribunal under the Act.
There are a host of such matters in which the Tribunal exercises
original or appellate jurisdiction.
33. It is noteworthy that the expression "for the determination of
any dispute, question or other matter relating to a wakf or wakf
property" appearing in Section 83(1) also appears in Section 85 of the
Act. Section 85 does not, however, exclude the jurisdiction of the Civil
Courts in respect of any or every question or disputes only because the
same relates to a wakf or a wakf property. Section 85 in terms provides
that the jurisdiction of the Civil Court shall stand excluded in relation
to only such matters as are required by or under this Act to be
determined by the Tribunal.
35. In the cases at hand the Act does not provide for any
proceedings before the Tribunal for determination of a dispute
concerning the eviction of a tenant in occupation of a wakf property or
the rights and obligations of the lessor and the lessees of such property.
A suit seeking eviction of the tenants from what is admittedly wakf
property could, therefore, be filed only before the Civil Court and not
before the Tribunal."
9. The Hon'ble Apex Court in a judgment rendered
in Civil Appeal Nos. 4250 - 4252 of 2014 arising out of
S.L.P. (Civil) Nos. 23157-23159 of 2012 - Faseela M.
Vs. Munnerul Islam Madrasa Committee & Anr. has yet
again reiterated the proposition which has been
propounded by the Hon'ble Apex Court in its para No. 9
dealt with issue as to for determination of a lease of a
tenant from a property belonging to the waqf is it triable by
the Civil Courts and not by the Tribunals created under the
Waqf Act.

10
"9. The question, for determination in these appeals, is
as to whether the suit for eviction by the landlord against
the tenant relating to waqf property is triable by the civil
court or the suit lies within the exclusive jurisdiction of the
Waqf Tribunal."
10. The Hon'ble Apex Court in the same judgment in
its para 11, while considering the scope of the Tribunal
created under the Waqf Act, 1995 as contemplated under
its Section 7 has yet again dealt with the said fact while
reading with Section 83 as well as Section 85 holding that
the suit for eviction of a leased property to a tenant would
be triable by the Civil Court and not by the Courts
/Tribunals created under the Waqf Act, 1995.
"11. In Ramesh Gobindram (Dead) through LRS. Vs.
Sugra Humayun Mirza Wakfi, this Court considered
Sections 6(1), 6(5), 7(1), 7(5), 83, 85 and few other
provisions of the Act and explained the jurisdiction of the
Waqf Tribunal vis-à-vis Civil Court. As regards the suit for
eviction against the tenant(s) of waqf property, the Court
held that such suit is triable by the Civil Court as it is not
covered by Sections 6 and 7 of the Act."
11. In a judgment reported and arising from this
Court, the learned Single Judge of this Court has held in
its para Nos. 12 and 13 of the judgment reported in 2011
(2) ARC 478 in Waqf Masjid Railway Station Jwalapur
Vs. Ashok Sethi and three others while dealing with the
competence of the Tribunal in relation to the determination
of inter se rights between the tenant and the landlord in a
proceedings for eviction. The Court held that the Tribunal
or District Judge as created under Section 83 of the Waqf
Act is not competent to deal with the situations of eviction
of a tenant.

11
"11. In the case at hand, there is no dispute between the
parties about the legal proposition as to the jurisdiction of
the Tribunal, involved in the present revision.
12. Without entering into the merits of the case and
considering the preliminary objection raised by the learned
counsel for the defendant-respondents on the point of
jurisdiction of the Tribunal, I am of the view that the
revisionist-plaintiff should have filed a suit before the
competent court for the eviction of the respondents and the
Tribunal/District Judge has no jurisdiction to entertain the
suit for eviction and possession filed by the plaintiff-revisionist. I am fortified in my view by the Apex Court
judgment in the case of Ramesh Gobindram vs. Sugra
Humayun Mirza Wakf [(2010) 8 SCALE, 698], wherein it
was held that eviction proceedings can only be decided by
the Civil Court and not by the Wakf Tribunal."
12. In that view of the matter, the argument as
extended by the learned counsel for the revisionist that the
plaintiffs should have invoked Section 83 of the Waqf Act
for seeking a relief of eviction of a tenant, is not acceptable
accordingly the said issue is decided against the tenant-revisionist.
13. Another argument which has been extended by
the learned counsel for the revisionist although not
pleaded in his written statement is to the extent that since
the rent was received by the plaintiff-respondent No. 2 in
an individual capacity, the relationship of landlord and
tenant, if any, would be between the plaintiff No. 2 and the
revisionist. This plea, yet again is not a plea which was
agitated by the revisionist before the learned trial court.
Further, this plea could not have been extended at this
stage for the reason being if the cause title of the suit itself
is scrutinized, the necessity for impleadment of plaintiff No.
2 was to represent a body which was registered under the

12
Act and acquired status of being a legal entity, and as
such the acceptance of the rent by plaintiff No. 2 was in
the official capacity of mutwalli who deals with financial
matter of a waqf under an authority vested in the office,
with which she was described in the cause title of the
plaint and not as an individual.
14. Hence, this issue too is unsustainable and is
decided against the revisionist because whatsoever the
transaction pertaining to the leased property of waqf was
being taken was taken at the behest of plaintiff No. 2 in the
capacity of mutwalli on behalf of the plaintiff No. 1, the
Waqf. Hence this issue too is decided against the
revisionist.
15. As far as issue No. 3 is concerned, the plea is
almost covered by issue No. 2, which has been decided
against the revisionist because the description of the
plaintiff No. 1 in the manner it was done was a legal
necessity.
16. Let us presume for a moment that this plea is
sustainable, in such an eventuality his argument pertaining
to issue No. 1 with regards to the import of Section 83 read
with Section 7 of the Act itself runs contrary to one
another. If he contends that the proceedings ought to have
been initiated under Section 83 of the Act, then he cannot
be permitted to take the plea as raised by him to the effect
that the plaintiff has impleaded the waqf to oust the

13
jurisdiction of Act No. 13 of 1972, at least by this
argument, the revision admits, tenancy of waqf; property
being of waqf and he being tenant of waqf.
17. Lastly, the learned counsel for the revisionist
has contended that the revisionist has made deposits
under Section 30 of Act No. 13 of 1972 and, as such he
cannot be treated as to be a defaulter for the purposes of
seeking a decree of eviction from the tenement in
question. The deposits under Section 30 which has been
made by the revisionist, though under law do not create
any right of defence in favour of the defendant because on
a simpliciter reading of Section 30 whatsoever deposit has
been made by the tenant before the Court is at his risk.
For convenience, Section 30 of U.P. Act No. 13 of 1972 is
quoted hereunder:-
"30. Deposit of rent in Court in certain
circumstances (1) If any person claiming to be a
tenant of a building tenders any amount as rent in
respect of the building to its alleged landlord and the
alleged landlord refuses to accept the same then the
former may deposit such amount in the prescribed
manner and continue to deposit any rent which he
alleges to be due for any subsequent period in respect
of such building until the landlord in the meantime
signifies by notice in writing to the tenant his willingness
to accept it.
(2) Where any bona fide doubt or dispute has arisen as
to the person who is entitled to receive any rent in
respect of any building, the tenant may likewise deposit
the rent stating the circumstances under which such
deposit is made and may, until such doubt has been
removed or such dispute has been settled by the
decision of any competent Court or by settlement
between the parties, continue to deposit the rent that

14
may subsequently become due in respect of such
building.
(3) The deposit referred to in sub-section (1), or sub-section (2) shall be made in the Court of the Munsif
having jurisdiction.
(4) On any deposit being made under sub-section (1),
the Court shall cause a notice of the deposit to be
served on the alleged landlord, and the amount of
deposit may be withdrawn by that person on application
made by him to the Court in that behalf.
(5) On a deposit being made under sub-section (2), the
Court shall cause notice of the deposit to be served on
the person or persons concerned and hold the amount
of the deposit for the benefit of the person who may be
found entitled to it by any competent Court or by a
settlement between the parties, and the same shall be
payable to such person.
(6) In respect of a deposit made as aforesaid, it shall be
deemed that the person depositing it has paid it on the
date of such deposit to the person in whose favour it is
deposited in the case referred to in sub-section (1) or to
the landlord in the case referred to in sub-section (2).
18. If this be so, he cannot be permitted to take
advantage of the fact that he has deposited under Section
30 hence he would be rendered immune from the decree
of eviction.
19. In the instant case what is to be seen is that the
suit itself was instituted by the plaintiff on 28.10.2009 and
the application under Section 30 has been filed thereafter.
Hence, it would not be having any bearing on the SCC
Suit.

15
20. The deposits which are claimed to have been
made by revisionist are under Section 30 of Act No. 13 of
1972. The U.P. Urban Building (Regulation of Letting, Rent
& Eviction), Act, 1972 has been amended as per
amendments made by U.P. Act No. 5 of 1995, made w.e.f.
26.09.1994 to the following effect in under Section 2(bbb)
"2. Exemption from Operation of Act - (1) Nothing
in this Act shall apply to the following, namely:-
(a) ............
(b) ............
(bb) ...........
(bbb) any building belonging to or vested in a waqf
including a waqf-alal-aulad
When the applicability of Rent Control Act is
ousted by under Section 2(bbb) from applicability of
Act or Waqf of property, and because under Section
30 being a provision provided under Act No. 13 of
1972, no benefit to the deposits made by revisionist
under Section 30 could be extended to him. Thus
deposit made under Section 30 is of no avail to the
revisionist.
21. Another argument which has been extended by
the learned counsel for the revisionist is that in view of the
amendment as has been made under Section 83 of the
Waqf Act to the following effect:-
"83. Subs. by Act 27 of 2013, S. 44(a) (w.e.f. 1-11-2013).
Prior to substitution it read as:

16
"(1) The State Government shall, by notification
in the Official Gazette, constitute as many Tribunals
as it may think fit, for the determination of any
dispute, question or other matter relating to a wakf or
wakf property under this Act and define the local
limits and jurisdiction under this Act of each of such
Tribunals."
22. The proceedings would be cognizable before the
Tribunal created under Section 83 of the Waqf Act. The
amendment which has been brought about under Section
83 is w.e.f. 01.11.2013.
23. According to the learned counsel for the plaintiff-respondent, the amendment which has been made are
procedural in nature, since it was classifying the nature of
dispute which could be agitated by the Tribunal, coupled
with the Notification as issued on 01.11.2013, the
substitution, which has been made under Section 83 since
being prospective in nature as having not made applicable
retrospectively, it will not apply to the proceedings in the
suit, which was instituted in the 2009 as the suit would be
determined on the basis of law prevailing at that point of
time.
24. To support his argument, learned counsel for the
respondent places reliance on para 5 & 6 of the judgment
reported in 2005(60) ALR 810 in Dido Ram Vs. First
Additional District Judge, Badaun and others":-
"5. On the same principle delivery of possession of
the encroached property by defendant to the plaintiff
will not take away the suit from the jurisdiction of the
Regular Civil Court in respect of the tenanted property.
Under section 20(C) C.P.C. every suit shall be

17
instituted in a Court within the local limits of whose
jurisdiction the cause of action wholly or in part arises.
It has been held in AIR 1957 Rajasthan 241 and AIR
1928 Madras 746 that where a Court once obtain
jurisdiction over a suit, it is not deprived of it by the
happening of subsequent events.
6. It has been held by the Full Bench Authority of
this Court in Manzurul Haq and another v. Hakim
Mohsin Ali, that the Court of Small Causes is a Court of
preferential jurisdiction and not of exclusive
jurisdiction."
25. This Court feels that even if the substitution
made on 01.11.2013 is logically scrutinized, it only deals
with the constitution of a Tribunal and the purpose for
which it is to be constituted and when the substitution
refers to a disputes, questions and other matters relating
to the waqf or waqf property, it would be read with co-relation with to the issues as referred in Section 7 of the
Act because there is no corresponding substitution made
under Section 7 by the amendment of 2013. Thus the
amendment on which the learned counsel for the
revisionist places reliance would not be of any benefit to
him.
26. The argument pertaining to the ouster of the
jurisdiction of the Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, 1887
which has been sought by the of learned counsel for the
revisionist would not be available to him for the reason if
entry four of Schedule II, which deals with the institution of
a suit by a lessor for eviction of a lessee from a building is
not ousted from cognizance by the Provincial Small

18
Causes Courts Act and thus the Suit would be tenable
before the Provincial Small Causes Courts Act.
27. No other point has been argued or pressed by
the learned counsel for the revisionist.
28. In that view of the matter, there is no merit in the
revision and the same is accordingly dismissed. No order
